claim: The power of electrophysiologically measured cortical activity decays with an approximately 1/fX function.
source: The power of electrophysiologically measured cortical activity decays with an approximately 1 /fX function.
evidence: This is a well-established characterization of cortical activity in the frequency domain, supported by scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The spectral exponent (X) is modulated by various factors such as age, cognitive states or psychiatric/neurological disorders.
source: The slope of this decay (i.e. the spectral exponent, X) is modulated by various factors such as age, cognitive states or psychiatric/neurological disorders.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research throughout the manuscript and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Similar effects for the spectral slope have been uncovered in the electrocardiogram (ECG).
source: Interestingly, a mostly parallel line of research has also uncovered similar effects for the spectral slope in the electrocardiogram (ECG).
evidence: This is supported by citations to ECG research mentioned in the introduction and by the literature analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The study analyzed a total of 1282 recordings of magnetoencephalography (MEG) resting state measurements with concurrent ECG in an age-diverse sample (18–88 years).
source: Focusing on well-established age-related changes in spectral slopes, we analyzed a total of 1282 recordings of magnetoencephalography (MEG) resting state measurements with concurrent ECG in an age-diverse sample (18–88 years).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data analyzed in the study, representing the experimental design and sample characteristics.

claim: The aperiodic signal recorded via surface electrodes/sensors originates from multiple physiological sources.
source: Using a diverse array of analytical approaches, we demonstrate that the aperiodic signal recorded via surface electrodes/sensors originates from multiple physiological sources.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the analyses conducted across multiple datasets and conditions.

claim: Common 'artifact' rejection approaches (i.e. ICA) may not be sufficient to separate cardiac from neural activity.
source: Furthermore, our results suggest that common 'artifact' rejection approaches (i.e. ICA) may not be sufficient to separate cardiac from neural activity.
evidence: This is based on the temporal response function analysis and residual ECG signal detection after ICA, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: Significant parts of age-related changes in aperiodic activity normally interpreted to be of neural origin can be explained by cardiac activity.
source: In particular, significant parts of age-related changes in aperiodic activity normally interpreted to be of neural origin can be explained by cardiac activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on the multiple regression analyses showing that cardiac components explain variance in age-related aperiodic changes.

claim: Changes (flattening/steepening) of the spectral slope with age are dependent on the recording site and investigated frequency range.
source: Moreover, our results suggest that changes (flattening/steepening) of the spectral slope with age are dependent on the recording site and investigated frequency range.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analyses across different frequency ranges and sensor locations shown in Figure 4.

claim: Aperiodic neural activity is omnipresent both in invasive (e.g. ECoG) and non-invasive (e.g. MEG/EEG) recordings of electrophysiological brain activity.
source: Aperiodic neural activity is omnipresent both in invasive (e.g. ECoG Miller et al., 2009) and non-invasive (e.g. MEG/EEG Demanuele et al., 2007; Pritchard, 1992) recordings of electrophysiological brain activity and even in hemodynamic responses (e.g. fMRI He et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research demonstrating aperiodic activity across recording modalities.

claim: Aperiodic activity is present in hemodynamic responses (e.g. fMRI).
source: Aperiodic neural activity is omnipresent both in invasive (e.g. ECoG Miller et al., 2009) and non-invasive (e.g. MEG/EEG Demanuele et al., 2007; Pritchard, 1992) recordings of electrophysiological brain activity and even in hemodynamic responses (e.g. fMRI He et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to He et al., 2010 demonstrating aperiodic activity in fMRI data.

claim: In the frequency domain, when visualized in log-log coordinates, aperiodic activity manifests as a linear decay in power with an increase in frequency.
source: In the frequency domain, when visualized in log-log coordinates (log-frequency/log-power), aperiodic activity manifests as a linear decay in power with an increase in frequency (Miller et al., 2009) (i.e. the spectral slope).
evidence: This is a fundamental characteristic of aperiodic activity supported by citation and established knowledge in the field.

claim: Aperiodic activity is meaningfully modulated by age.
source: Several studies have shown that aperiodic neural activity is meaningfully modulated by various factors, such as age (Voytek et al., 2015), cognitive state (e.g. awake vs. sleep He et al., 2010) and disorders like Parkinson's disease and epilepsy (Ghinda et al., 2020; Mostile et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Voytek et al., 2015 and other studies demonstrating age-related modulation.

claim: Aperiodic activity is meaningfully modulated by cognitive state (e.g. awake vs. sleep).
source: Several studies have shown that aperiodic neural activity is meaningfully modulated by various factors, such as age (Voytek et al., 2015), cognitive state (e.g. awake vs. sleep He et al., 2010) and disorders like Parkinson's disease and epilepsy (Ghinda et al., 2020; Mostile et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to He et al., 2010 demonstrating cognitive state modulation.

claim: Aperiodic activity is meaningfully modulated by disorders like Parkinson's disease and epilepsy.
source: Several studies have shown that aperiodic neural activity is meaningfully modulated by various factors, such as age (Voytek et al., 2015), cognitive state (e.g. awake vs. sleep He et al., 2010) and disorders like Parkinson's disease and epilepsy (Ghinda et al., 2020; Mostile et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ghinda et al., 2020 and Mostile et al., 2019 demonstrating disorder-related modulation.

claim: Aperiodic activity is present in recordings of cardiac activity measured using ECG.
source: However, aperiodic activity is not only present in recordings of neural activity, but also part of other physiological signals such as cardiac and muscle activity, commonly measured using electrocardiography (ECG Saul et al., 1988) and electromyography (Kozhemiako et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Saul et al., 1988 demonstrating aperiodic activity in ECG recordings.

claim: Aperiodic activity is present in recordings of muscle activity measured using electromyography.
source: However, aperiodic activity is not only present in recordings of neural activity, but also part of other physiological signals such as cardiac and muscle activity, commonly measured using electrocardiography (ECG Saul et al., 1988) and electromyography (Kozhemiako et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kozhemiako et al., 2022 demonstrating aperiodic activity in EMG recordings.

claim: Aperiodic activity measured using ECG is modulated by aging.
source: Interestingly, and mostly overlooked by the neuroscience community (see Figure 1C), aperiodic activity measured using ECG (often referred to as power law or 1/f activity) is modulated by similar factors as neural aperiodic activity, including aging (Beckers et al., 2006), different cognitive states (e.g. awake vs. sleep Kozhemiako et al., 2022; Penzel et al., 2003) and disorders such as Parkinson's disease and epilepsy (Ansakorpi et al., 2002; Haapaniemi et al., 2001; see also Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beckers et al., 2006 and demonstrated in the manuscript's own analyses shown in Figure 2.

claim: Aperiodic activity measured using ECG is modulated by different cognitive states (e.g. awake vs. sleep).
source: Interestingly, and mostly overlooked by the neuroscience community (see Figure 1C), aperiodic activity measured using ECG (often referred to as power law or 1/f activity) is modulated by similar factors as neural aperiodic activity, including aging (Beckers et al., 2006), different cognitive states (e.g. awake vs. sleep Kozhemiako et al., 2022; Penzel et al., 2003) and disorders such as Parkinson's disease and epilepsy (Ansakorpi et al., 2002; Haapaniemi et al., 2001; see also Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kozhemiako et al., 2022 and Penzel et al., 2003 demonstrating cognitive state modulation in ECG.

claim: Aperiodic activity measured using ECG is modulated by disorders such as Parkinson's disease and epilepsy.
source: Interestingly, and mostly overlooked by the neuroscience community (see Figure 1C), aperiodic activity measured using ECG (often referred to as power law or 1/f activity) is modulated by similar factors as neural aperiodic activity, including aging (Beckers et al., 2006), different cognitive states (e.g. awake vs. sleep Kozhemiako et al., 2022; Penzel et al., 2003) and disorders such as Parkinson's disease and epilepsy (Ansakorpi et al., 2002; Haapaniemi et al., 2001; see also Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ansakorpi et al., 2002 and Haapaniemi et al., 2001 demonstrating disorder-related modulation in ECG.

claim: Via volume conduction, cardiac activity can be captured in both invasive and non-invasive recordings of neural activity.
source: Furthermore, it is well-known that, via volume conduction, cardiac activity can also be captured in both invasive and non-invasive recordings of neural activity (Dirlich et al., 1997; Jousmäki and Hari, 1996; Kern et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dirlich et al., 1997; Jousmäki and Hari, 1996; Kern et al., 2013 and represents established knowledge.

claim: It is considered best practice to measure and remove cardiac activity from M/EEG recordings.
source: Hence, it is also considered best practice to measure and remove cardiac activity from M/EEG recordings (Gross et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gross et al., 2013 and represents a methodological standard in the field.

claim: Only 17.1% of EEG studies explicitly mention that cardiac activity was removed.
source: However, an analysis of openly accessible M/EEG articles that investigate aperiodic activity (NArticles = 279; see Methods - Literature Analysis for further details) revealed that only 17.1% of EEG studies explicitly mention that cardiac activity was removed and only 16.5% measure ECG (45.9% of MEG studies removed cardiac activity and 31.1% of MEG studies mention that ECG was measured; see Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is based on the literature analysis conducted by the authors, with results shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Only 16.5% of EEG studies measure ECG.
source: However, an analysis of openly accessible M/EEG articles that investigate aperiodic activity (NArticles = 279; see Methods - Literature Analysis for further details) revealed that only 17.1% of EEG studies explicitly mention that cardiac activity was removed and only 16.5% measure ECG (45.9% of MEG studies removed cardiac activity and 31.1% of MEG studies mention that ECG was measured; see Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is based on the literature analysis conducted by the authors, with results shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: 45.9% of MEG studies removed cardiac activity.
source: However, an analysis of openly accessible M/EEG articles that investigate aperiodic activity (NArticles = 279; see Methods - Literature Analysis for further details) revealed that only 17.1% of EEG studies explicitly mention that cardiac activity was removed and only 16.5% measure ECG (45.9% of MEG studies removed cardiac activity and 31.1% of MEG studies mention that ECG was measured; see Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is based on the literature analysis conducted by the authors, with results shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: 31.1% of MEG studies mention that ECG was measured.
source: However, an analysis of openly accessible M/EEG articles that investigate aperiodic activity (NArticles = 279; see Methods - Literature Analysis for further details) revealed that only 17.1% of EEG studies explicitly mention that cardiac activity was removed and only 16.5% measure ECG (45.9% of MEG studies removed cardiac activity and 31.1% of MEG studies mention that ECG was measured; see Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is based on the literature analysis conducted by the authors, with results shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Investigations of aperiodic activity vary strongly by both the upper and lower bounds and the general width of the analyzed frequency ranges.
source: Additionally, investigations of aperiodic activity vary strongly by both the upper and lower bounds and the general width of the analyzed frequency ranges (Figure 1G-I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the literature analysis shown in Figure 1G-I.

claim: Physiological signals (e.g. cardiac activity) may have varying impacts across frequency ranges—for instance, exerting a stronger influence on lower frequencies than on higher ones.
source: This further complicates the comparison of results across studies as physiological signals (e.g. cardiac activity) may have varying impacts across frequency ranges—for instance, exerting a stronger influence on lower frequencies than on higher ones.
evidence: This is an inference based on the frequency-dependent effects observed in the study's analyses.

claim: The spectral slope flattened with age over a vast amount of different frequency ranges in ECG recordings.
source: Our results show that the spectral slope flattened with age over a vast amount of different frequency ranges (see Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on the analysis of ECG data from four age-diverse populations, with results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: An age-related steepening of the spectral slope was observed in one dataset (ECG Dataset 3 - CamCAN) in the low-frequency range (0.25–12 Hz).
source: However, we also noted an age-related steepening of the spectral slope in one dataset (ECG Dataset 3 - CamCAN) in the low-frequency range (0.25–12 Hz, see Discussion).
evidence: This is based on the analysis of ECG Dataset 3, representing an exception to the general flattening trend.

claim: Spectral slopes in lower frequency ranges (0.25–20 Hz) were more consistently related to heart rate variability indices (39.4–74.6% of all investigated indices) than spectral slopes in higher frequency ranges (16–30.01% of all investigated indices).
source: Overall, spectral slopes in lower frequency ranges were more consistently related to heart rate variability indices (39.4–74.6% percent of all investigated indices) than spectral slopes in higher frequency ranges (16–30.01% percent of all investigated indices; see Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on the exploratory analysis relating spectral slopes to 90 different indices of heart rate variability, with results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In the lower frequency ranges (0.25–20 Hz), spectral slopes were consistently related to most measures of heart rate variability including fractal, multifractal, time and frequency domain analyses as well as indices extracted from the Poincaré plot.
source: In the lower frequency ranges (0.25–20 Hz), spectral slopes were consistently related to most measures of heart rate variability; that is significant effects were detected in all four datasets (see Figure 2D). This includes fractal, multifractal, time and frequency domain analyses as well as indices extracted from the Poincaré plot.
evidence: This is based on the analysis relating spectral slopes to heart rate variability measures, with results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In the higher frequency ranges (10–145 Hz), spectral slopes were most consistently related to fractal and time domain indices of heart rate variability, but not so much to frequency-domain indices assessing spectral power in frequency ranges <0.4 Hz.
source: In the higher frequency ranges (10–145 Hz), spectral slopes were most consistently related to fractal and time domain indices of heart rate variability, but not so much to frequency-domain indices assessing spectral power in frequency ranges <0.4 Hz.
evidence: This is based on the analysis relating spectral slopes to heart rate variability measures across different frequency ranges.

claim: Spectral slopes >10 Hz carry meaningful information about cardiac activity that is largely distinct from the frequency-domain information that is commonly investigated using ECG.
source: This suggests that spectral slopes >10 Hz carry meaningful information about cardiac activity that is largely distinct from the frequency-domain information that is commonly investigated using ECG.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential relationships between spectral slopes in different frequency ranges and heart rate variability measures.

claim: The direction of the association between age and aperiodic ECG activity is largely identical to that reported for age and aperiodic EEG activity.
source: Importantly, the direction of the association between age and aperiodic ECG activity is largely identical to that reported for age and aperiodic EEG activity (Donoghue et al., 2020; Voytek et al., 2015), motivating the investigation of these relationships in combined neural and cardiac measurements.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the current ECG results with prior EEG/ECoG findings cited in the manuscript.

claim: If ECG components are not removed via ICA, the ECG signal is captured equally strong at zero-time lags both in EEG and MEG recordings.
source: Our results show that if ECG components are not removed via ICA, the ECG signal is captured equally strong at zero-time lags both in EEG and MEG recordings (see Figure 3A,C,D).
evidence: This is based on the temporal response function analysis shown in Figure 3A,C,D.

claim: After removing ECG-related components from the data, TRF peaks emerged (although reduced) at zero-time lags in EEG, but not in MEG recordings.
source: Even after removing ECG-related components from the data, TRF peaks emerged (although reduced) at zero-time lags in EEG, but not in MEG recordings (see Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is based on the temporal response function analysis shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Reconstruction (decoding) of the ECG signal was reduced, but remained above chance even after rejecting the ICA signal using ECG both in MEG and EEG recordings.
source: Furthermore, reconstruction (decoding) of the ECG signal was reduced, but remained above chance even after rejecting the ICA signal using ECG both in MEG and EEG recordings (r>0).
evidence: This is based on the decoding analysis shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The presence of the ECG signal was more pronounced in EEG compared to MEG recordings, after removing ECG-related components.
source: Interestingly, the presence of the ECG signal was more pronounced in EEG compared to MEG recordings, after removing ECG-related components (βstandardized (EEG > MEG)=0.97, HDI = [0.42, 1.52]; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of residual ECG signal in EEG vs MEG after ICA, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ECG-related components extracted from MEG recordings were more related to the ECG signal than the components extracted from the EEG.
source: Additionally, ECG-related components extracted from MEG recordings were more related to the ECG signal than the components extracted from the EEG (βstandardized (EEG > MEG)=–0.76, HDI = [-1.35,–0.18]; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of ECG component correlations in MEG vs EEG, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Neural and cardiac activity are more difficult to separate in EEG as opposed to MEG recordings.
source: These results show that (A) residual ECG activity remains in surface neural recordings, even after applying a very sensitive threshold to detect and remove ECG components via ICA and (B) neural and cardiac activity are more difficult to separate in EEG as opposed to MEG recordings (see Figure 3A,C,D), resulting in more residual (after ICA) ECG-related activity in EEG recordings.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TRF and decoding analyses showing more residual ECG in EEG after ICA.

claim: Even if the PQRST-Complex is barely visible in the combined time domain signal, the resulting power spectrum can be heavily affected by simulated changes in aperiodic cardiac activity.
source: Combining both cardiac and neural time series data shows that even if the PQRST-Complex is barely visible in the combined time domain signal, the resulting power spectrum can be heavily affected by simulated changes in aperiodic cardiac activity (see Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 3F,G demonstrating the impact of cardiac aperiodic activity on combined spectra.

claim: Over a broad amount of individual fitting ranges and sensors, aging resulted in a steepening of spectral slopes across conditions.
source: This analysis, which is depicted in Figure 4, shows that over a broad amount of individual fitting ranges and sensors, aging resulted in a steepening of spectral slopes across conditions (see Figure 4B) with 'steepening effects' observed in 25% of the slope fits in MEGECG not rejected, 0.5% in MEGECG rejected, and 60% for MEGECG components.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of age effects on spectral slopes across multiple conditions and frequency ranges, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Steepening effects were observed in 25% of the slope fits in MEGECG not rejected, 0.5% in MEGECG rejected, and 60% for MEGECG components.
source: This analysis, which is depicted in Figure 4, shows that over a broad amount of individual fitting ranges and sensors, aging resulted in a steepening of spectral slopes across conditions (see Figure 4B) with 'steepening effects' observed in 25% of the slope fits in MEGECG not rejected, 0.5% in MEGECG rejected, and 60% for MEGECG components.
evidence: This is based on quantification of effects across processing options shown in Figure 4.

claim: Null effects were observed in 13% of the options for MEGECG not rejected, 30% in MEGECG rejected, and 7% for MEGECG components.
source: The second largest category of effects was 'null effects' in 13% of the options for MEGECG not rejected, 30% in MEGECG rejected, and 7% for MEGECG components.
evidence: This is based on quantification of null effects across processing options.

claim: Flattening effects in the spectral slope were found for 0.16% of the processing options in MEGECG not rejected, 0.3% in MEGECG rejected, and 0.46% in MEGECG components.
source: However, we also found 'flattening effects' in the spectral slope for 0.16% of the processing options in MEGECG not rejected, 0.3% in MEGECG rejected, and 0.46% in MEGECG components.
evidence: This is based on quantification of flattening effects across processing options.

claim: Age-related flattening of the spectral slope occurred mainly at centrally and parietally located electrodes in lower frequency ranges between 0.5 and 45 Hz.
source: However, despite the large amount of age-related steepening effects, we also noted age-related flattening in spectral slopes that occurred mainly at centrally and parietally located electrodes in lower frequency ranges between 0.5 and 45 Hz (see Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on the spatial and frequency-specific analysis of flattening effects shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The observed flattening results overlap both in frequency range and recording site with some of the results previously reported in the literature.
source: Importantly, these results overlap both in frequency range and recording site with some of the results previously reported in the literature (Voytek et al., 2015; Tröndle et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the current findings with prior literature cited in the manuscript.

claim: A flattening of spectral slopes with age can be observed at some of the previously reported frequency ranges (~0.5–45 Hz) and spatial locations (on central, parietal, and occipital sensors).
source: In sum, this analysis suggests that a flattening of spectral slopes with age can be observed at some of the previously reported frequency ranges (~0.5–45 Hz) and spatial locations (on central, parietal, and occipital sensors).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings regarding flattening effects and their spatial/frequency characteristics.

claim: Age-related flattening of the spectral slope represented only 0.3% of effects across all processing settings (conditions, sensors, and frequency ranges).
source: However, these results represented only 0.3% of effects across all processing settings (conditions, sensors, and frequency ranges).
evidence: This is based on quantification of flattening effects across all processing options.

claim: When restrictively looking only at the investigated frequency ranges between 0.5 and 50 Hz, only 1.2% (0.4% after maxfilter) of effects across these residual settings were showing an age-related flattening of the spectral slope.
source: Even when restrictively looking only at the investigated frequency ranges between 0.5 and 50 Hz, only 1.2% (0.4% after maxfilter see Figure 4—figure supplement 7) of effects across these residual settings were showing an age-related flattening of the spectral slope.
evidence: This is based on quantification of flattening effects in a restricted frequency range, with maxfilter results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claim: Age-related flattening of the spectral slope is tied to specific recording sites and frequency ranges.
source: This suggests that age-related flattening of the spectral slope is tied to specific recording sites and frequency ranges.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial and frequency-specific patterns of flattening effects observed in the data.

claim: Age-related steepening/flattening of the spectral slope in the MEG is both dependent on the investigated frequency range and the sensor selection.
source: So far, we have shown that age-related steepening/flattening of the spectral slope in the MEG is both dependent on the investigated frequency range and the sensor selection.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the analyses across different frequency ranges and sensor locations.

claim: Aperiodic brain activity (MEGECG rejected), at some frequency ranges, changes with age independently of cardiac activity (MEGECG component) and vice versa.
source: Some of the observed age-related flattening and steepening effects were solely present in one of the tested conditions (see Figure 4H). This suggests that aperiodic brain activity (MEGECG rejected), at some frequency ranges, changes with age independently of cardiac activity (MEGECG component) and vice versa.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of condition-specific effects shown in Figure 4H.

claim: When adding both MEGECG component and MEGECG rejected as predictors, age-related flattening effects were reduced, yielding no longer significant flattening results.
source: The analysis revealed that when adding both MEGECG component and MEGECG rejected as predictors, age-related flattening effects were reduced, yielding no longer significant flattening results (see Figure 4B; upper panel).
evidence: This is based on the multiple regression analysis shown in Figure 4I (upper panel).

claim: In the case of the observed steepening effects, significant effects for MEGECG components remained in 98.75% of the tested frequency ranges.
source: However, in case of the observed steepening effects, significant effects for MEGECG components remained in 98.75% of the tested frequency ranges (see Figure 4B; lower panel).
evidence: This is based on the multiple regression analysis shown in Figure 4I (lower panel).

claim: Whether or not aperiodic brain activity changes independently from cardiac activity with age depends on the recording site and the selected frequency range.
source: In sum, these results suggest that whether or not aperiodic brain activity changes independently from cardiac activity with age depends on the recording site and the selected frequency range.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the frequency- and location-dependent patterns of cardiac and neural contributions to age-related changes.

claim: On the grand average across channels, the spectral slope was slightly steeper in older subjects even before spectral parametrization.
source: First, we conducted a median split of age to compare the raw power spectra averaged across channels (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1). This shows that on the grand average across channels, the spectral slope was slightly steeper in older subjects even before spectral parametrization.
evidence: This is based on the control analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: On the grand average across sensors, slightly stronger steepening effects were observed for the MEGECG not rejected data compared to MEGECG rejected when not cleaning the data using SSS and vice versa.
source: On the grand average across sensors, slightly stronger steepening effects were observed for the MEGECG not rejected data compared to MEGECG rejected when not cleaning the data using SSS and vice versa (see Figure 4—figure supplement 5 for a comparison).
evidence: This is based on the comparison of results with and without SSS shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: On the level of single sensors, the application of SSS resulted in a further reduction of both flattening and steepening effects in all conditions except for MEGECG components, where we noted a 20% increase in steepening effects.
source: On the level of single sensors, the application of SSS resulted in a further reduction of both flattening and steepening effects in all conditions except for MEGECG components, where we noted a 20% increase in steepening effects (see Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is based on the single-sensor analysis with SSS shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claim: The age-related steepening effects occur robustly in the MEG.
source: While all these control analyses indicate that the age-related steepening effects occur robustly in the MEG, it is unclear whether they can be exclusively attributed to cardiac activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the multiple control analyses conducted.

claim: The topography of the observed steepening effects is present across the scalp and prominent at frontal and temporal sensors around the MEG helmet.
source: Crucially, the topography of the observed steepening effects is present across the scalp and prominent at frontal and temporal sensors around the MEG helmet (albeit also observable at central locations; see MEGECG Components).
evidence: This is based on the spatial distribution of steepening effects observed in the analyses.

claim: Head movements increased significantly with aging.
source: While head movements increased significantly with aging (βstandardized=0.23, HDI = [0.18, 0.28], see Figure 4—figure supplement 8), it was not sufficient to explain the observed steepening or flattening effects in the spectral slope (see Figure 4—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is based on the control analysis using head movement as a covariate, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claim: Head movements were not sufficient to explain the observed steepening or flattening effects in the spectral slope.
source: While head movements increased significantly with aging (βstandardized=0.23, HDI = [0.18, 0.28], see Figure 4—figure supplement 8), it was not sufficient to explain the observed steepening or flattening effects in the spectral slope (see Figure 4—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is based on the control analysis using head movement as a covariate, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claim: There were no significant age-related steepening/flattening across the investigated frequency ranges in vertical and horizontal EOG channels.
source: We further investigated age-related changes to the spectral slope of the vertical and horizontal EOG channels indicating no significant age-related steepening/flattening across the investigated frequency ranges (see Figure 4—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is based on the control analysis of EOG channels shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claim: The discrepancy between the current findings and previous findings showing flattening can potentially be explained by multiple factors including physiologically measured 1/f noise differently affecting magnetic and electric recording devices, preprocessing choices, fitting ranges for the 1/f slope, electrode selection etc.
source: This discrepancy can potentially be explained by multiple factors including physiologically measured 1 /f noise differently affecting magnetic and electric recording devices (Dehghani et al., 2010), preprocessing choices, fitting ranges for the 1 /f slope, electrode selection etc. (see discussion).
evidence: This is speculation about potential explanations for the discrepancy, with citation to Dehghani et al., 2010.

claim: A consistent flattening of the aperiodic slope for cardiac activity was observed in the delay period of a working memory task.
source: Interestingly, akin to the EEG results reported by Donoghue et al., 2020, we observed a consistent flattening of the aperiodic slope for cardiac activity in the delay period (see Figure 5B,D; βstandardized=0.23, HDI = [0.16, 0.32]).
evidence: This is based on the working memory analysis shown in Figure 5B,D.

claim: The flattening effect of the slope was modulated by cognitive load.
source: Furthermore, upon comparing the change of slope relative to the baseline period across different levels of co,gnitive load we noticed that the flattening effect of the slope was modulated by cognitive load (see Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on the working memory analysis comparing different load conditions shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The slope flattened the most in the condition with the highest working memory load (13 items).
source: The slope flattened the most in the condition with the highest working memory load (13 items; βstandardized=0.42, HDI = [0.33, 0.52]), followed by the high load (9 items; βstandardized=0.39, HDI = [0.29, 0.48]) and the low load condition (5 items; βstandardized=0.25, HDI = [0.15, 0.35]).
evidence: This is based on the working memory analysis comparing different load conditions.

claim: Previous research has shown scaling differences in the spectral slope between MEG and EEG recordings.
source: Previous research has shown scaling differences in the spectral slope between MEG and EEG recordings (Dehghani et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dehghani et al., 2010.

claim: These scaling differences are partly widespread (overall flatter sloped spectra in MEG data) and partly regionally specific (steeper sloped spectra at vertex in MEG compared to EEG recordings and vice versa at frontal regions).
source: These scaling differences are partly widespread (overall flatter sloped spectra in MEG data) and partly regionally specific (steeper sloped spectra at vertex in MEG compared to EEG recordings and vice versa at frontal regions).
evidence: This is based on prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: These observations have been linked to non-resistive properties of tissue (i.e. the propagation of the electric field through tissue is frequency dependent).
source: These observations have been linked to non-resistive properties of tissue (i.e. the propagation of the electric field through tissue is frequency dependent Dehghani et al., 2010; Bedard et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dehghani et al., 2010 and Bedard et al., 2017.

claim: Magnetic field recordings are not distorted by the tissue conductivity of the scalp, skull, cerebrospinal fluid, and brain.
source: This differently affects the signal recorded using MEG and EEG, as magnetic field recordings are not distorted by the tissue conductivity of the scalp, skull, cerebrospinal fluid, and brain (Singh, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Singh, 2014 and represents established knowledge about MEG vs EEG.

claim: Under the hypothesis that frequency scaling differences may emerge in relation to the space/frequency structure of the recorded activity, lower frequencies are suggested to involve synchronous activity in larger patches of cortex, whereas higher frequencies involve synchronous activity in smaller cortical patches.
source: An alternative, but not exclusive, hypothesis suggests that even under the assumption of a purely resistive medium (which is unlikely Bedard et al., 2022; Gomes et al., 2016), frequency scaling differences between MEG and EEG may emerge in relation to the space/frequency structure of the recorded activity (Bénar et al., 2019). Under this hypothesis, lower frequencies are suggested to involve synchronous activity in larger patches of cortex, whereas higher frequencies involve synchronous activity in smaller cortical patches.
evidence: This is based on the hypothesis proposed by Bénar et al., 2019.

claim: EEG typically integrates activity over larger volumes than MEG, resulting in differently shaped spectra across both recording methods.
source: Bénar et al., 2019 demonstrate that EEG typically integrates activity over larger volumes than MEG, resulting in differently shaped spectra across both recording methods.
evidence: This is based on the findings of Bénar et al., 2019.

claim: During aging, both changes in conductive tissue properties and functional connectivity occur.
source: During aging, both changes in conductive tissue properties (Mohammed et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 2018) and functional connectivity occur (Deery et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mohammed et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 2018; and Deery et al., 2023.

claim: An interaction between several factors that differently affect MEG and EEG (e.g. age-related changes in non-resistive properties of tissue and in functional connectivity) may potentially explain differently shaped spectra in MEG compared to EEG recordings.
source: Hypothetically, an interaction between several factors that differently affect MEG and EEG (e.g. age-related changes in non-resistive properties of tissue and in functional connectivity) may therefore potentially explain differently shaped spectra in MEG compared to EEG recordings.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms explaining the observed differences.

claim: Aperiodic activity may not change strictly linearly as we are ageing, and studies looking at younger age groups may capture different aspects of aging (e.g. brain maturation) than those looking at older subjects.
source: Differences in electric and magnetic field recordings aside, aperiodic activity may not change strictly linearly as we are ageing, and studies looking at younger age groups (e.g. <22; Tröndle et al., 2022) may capture different aspects of aging (e.g. brain maturation) than those looking at older subjects (>18 years; our sample).
evidence: This is speculation about potential non-linear age effects, with citation to Tröndle et al., 2022.

claim: A recent report shows some first evidence of an interesting putatively non-linear relationship with age in the sensorimotor cortex for resting recordings.
source: A recent report even shows some first evidence of an interesting putatively non-linear relationship with age in the sensorimotor cortex for resting recordings (Cross et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cross et al., 2024.

claim: An age-related steepening of the ECG was only noted at a frequency range between ~0.25 and 12 Hz making it an unlikely explanation of all the effects detected in the MEG that span frequency ranges vastly exceeding the 0.25–12 Hz range.
source: However, an age-related steepening of the ECG was only noted at a frequency range between ~0.25 and 12 Hz making it an unlikely explanation of all the effects we detected in the MEG that span frequency ranges vastly exceeding the 0.25–12 Hz range.
evidence: This is an inference based on the frequency-specific patterns observed in ECG and MEG data.

claim: The slope of the power spectrum can be very sensitive to different preprocessing decisions that may emphasize different aspects of (neuro-)physiological activity.
source: The frequency dependence of the flattening/steepening effects (see Figure 4) suggests that the slope of the power spectrum can be very sensitive to different preprocessing decisions that may emphasize different aspects of (neuro-)physiological activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed sensitivity of results to different processing choices.

claim: Separating ECG-related components from neural activity using ICA seems to work worse in EEG compared to MEG recordings.
source: Furthermore, separating ECG-related components from neural activity using ICA seems to work worse in EEG compared to MEG recordings (see Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is based on the TRF analysis showing more residual ECG in EEG after ICA, shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Difficulties in removing ECG-related components from EEG signals via ICA might be attributable to various reasons such as the number of available sensors or assumptions related to the non-Gaussianity of the underlying sources.
source: Difficulties in removing ECG-related components from EEG signals via ICA might be attributable to various reasons such as the number of available sensors or assumptions related to the non-Gaussianity of the underlying sources.
evidence: This is speculation about potential reasons for the observed differences in ICA effectiveness.

claim: The effectiveness of an ICA crucially depends on the quality of the extracted components.
source: Additionally, it is worth noting that the effectiveness of an ICA crucially depends on the quality of the extracted components (Bailey et al., 2023; Bailey, 2024) and even widely suggested settings, for example high-pass filtering at 1 Hz before fitting an ICA may not be universally applicable (see supplementary material of Bailey, 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bailey et al., 2023 and Bailey, 2024.

claim: Previous work has shown that a linked mastoid reference alone was particularly effective in reducing the impact of ECG-related activity on aperiodic activity measured using EEG.
source: Previous work (Kozhemiako et al., 2022; Lendner et al., 2020) has shown that a linked mastoid reference alone was particularly effective in reducing the impact of ECG-related activity on aperiodic activity measured using EEG.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kozhemiako et al., 2022 and Lendner et al., 2020.

claim: Depending on the montage, referencing can induce ambiguities to the measured EEG signal.
source: However, it should be considered that depending on the montage, referencing can induce ambiguities to the measured EEG signal.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about EEG referencing.

claim: Linked mastoid referencing can distort temporal activity.
source: Linked mastoid referencing, for instance, can distort temporal activity (Feindel et al., 2009), which is unproblematic in studies focusing on activity on central electrodes (Kozhemiako et al., 2022; Lendner et al., 2020), but should be considered when focusing on activity from other recording sites (Yao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Feindel et al., 2009, Kozhemiako et al., 2022, Lendner et al., 2020, and Yao et al., 2019.

claim: The aperiodic signal recorded non-invasively originates from multiple physiological sources.
source: Our study investigated age-related changes in aperiodic activity using MEG and found that these changes vary depending on the frequency range and recording site. Specifically, some changes were found to be uniquely linked to either cardiac or brain activity, while others were present in both signals (Figure 4H). Interestingly, some of these shared effects could be attributed to cardiac activity (see Figure 4I). However, some effects appeared to be equally influential in explaining age-related changes in both cardiac and brain activity, such that the individual effects disappeared when analyzed jointly (see Figure 4I, upper panel). These findings underscore the complexity of analyzing aperiodic activity, indicating that the aperiodic signal recorded non-invasively originates from multiple physiological sources.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analyses showing different patterns of cardiac and neural contributions across conditions.

claim: Neural and vascular processes are known to interact with each other.
source: These shared effects are particularly interesting, as they suggest that a common mechanism across physiological signals exists that underlies age-related changes of aperiodic activity. In fact, neural and vascular processes are known to interact with each other (Takarada-Iemata et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Takarada-Iemata et al., 2019.

claim: Cardiovascular activity, in the form of the ECG, is captured in M/EEG recordings via volume conduction.
source: Cardiovascular activity, in the form of the ECG, is also captured in M/EEG recordings (via volume conduction; see Figure 3A-D).
evidence: This is based on the TRF analysis shown in Figure 3A-D and represents established knowledge.

claim: A current popular hypothesis states that the generative process underlying aperiodic neural activity is mainly attributed to differences in the ratio between excitatory (AMPA) and inhibitory (GABA) currents that influence the slope of the neural power spectrum.
source: For example, a current popular hypothesis states that the generative process underlying aperiodic neural activity is mainly attributed to differences in the ratio between excitatory (AMPA) and inhibitory (GABA) currents that influence the slope of the neural power spectrum (Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on the hypothesis proposed by Gao et al., 2017.

claim: Excitatory currents such as AMPA decay faster than inhibitory currents like GABA.
source: Excitatory currents such as AMPA decay faster than inhibitory currents like GABA.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about neurotransmitter kinetics.

claim: Flatter power spectra may be indicative of the presence of more excitatory than inhibitory currents and vice versa (steeper sloped power spectra).
source: This means that flatter power spectra may be indicative of the presence of more excitatory than inhibitory currents and vice versa (steeper sloped power spectra Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on the hypothesis proposed by Gao et al., 2017.

claim: GABAergic drugs like propofol modulate the slope of electrophysiologically measured power spectra.
source: This theory is (in part) based on research showing that GABAergic drugs like propofol (Gao et al., 2017) and glutamatergic drugs like ketamine (Waschke et al., 2021) modulate the slope of electrophysiologically measured power spectra.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gao et al., 2017 and Waschke et al., 2021.

claim: Glutamatergic drugs like ketamine modulate the slope of electrophysiologically measured power spectra.
source: This theory is (in part) based on research showing that GABAergic drugs like propofol (Gao et al., 2017) and glutamatergic drugs like ketamine (Waschke et al., 2021) modulate the slope of electrophysiologically measured power spectra.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Waschke et al., 2021.

claim: Propofol and ketamine not only influence neural activity, but also influence heart rate variability.
source: However, propofol and ketamine not only influence neural activity, but also influence heart rate variability (a core component of the ECG Goddard et al., 2021; Kanaya et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goddard et al., 2021 and Kanaya et al., 2003.

claim: Previous work has shown that propofol-induced changes to the spectral slope were still present in EEG recordings after using ICA to reject ECG components from the data.
source: Previous work has shown that propofol-induced changes to the spectral slope were still present in EEG recordings after using ICA to reject ECG components from the data (Lendner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lendner et al., 2020.

claim: Cardiac activity remains in EEG signals even after separating cardiac from neural sources using an ICA with a very sensitive rejection criterion.
source: However, our results suggest that cardiac activity remains in EEG signals even after separating cardiac from neural sources using an ICA with a very sensitive rejection criterion (see Figure 3A-D).
evidence: This is based on the TRF analysis shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: It is plausible that drug-induced effects on aperiodic 'neural' activity can still be conflated by cardiac activity.
source: It is therefore plausible that drug-induced effects on aperiodic "neural" activity can still be conflated by cardiac activity.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings about residual cardiac activity after ICA.

claim: Muscle activity can be captured in (non-)invasive recordings and may drastically influence measures of the spectral slope.
source: It is worth noting that, apart from cardiac activity, muscle activity can also be captured in (non-)invasive recordings and may drastically influence measures of the spectral slope (Fitzgibbon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fitzgibbon et al., 2016.

claim: Cardiac activity is captured on ECoG.
source: Given that cardiac activity is also captured on, for example ECoG (Kern et al., 2013), an influence is not unlikely depending on the strength of cardiac activity relative to the measured neural activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kern et al., 2013.

claim: Previously suspected periodic age-related changes in alpha power may actually be attributable to differences in aperiodic activity.
source: This has, for instance, revealed that previously suspected periodic age-related changes in alpha power may actually be attributable to differences in aperiodic activity (Donoghue et al., 2020; Merkin et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Donoghue et al., 2020 and Merkin et al., 2023.

claim: Whether or not periodic activity (after detection) should be detrended using approaches like FOOOF or IRASA still remains disputed, as incorrectly detrending the data may cause larger errors than not detrending at all.
source: However, whether or not periodic activity (after detection) should be detrended using approaches like FOOOF or IRASA still remains disputed, as incorrectly detrending the data may cause larger errors than not detrending at all (Brake et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brake et al., 2024.

claim: Changes in aperiodic activity of peripheral and neural signals are co-modulated by similar traits, states, and disorders.
source: Changes in aperiodic activity of peripheral and neural signals are co-modulated by similar traits, states, and disorders.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the literature analysis and the manuscript's own analyses.

claim: Separating physiological from neural sources using an ICA is no guarantee that peripheral physiological activity is fully removed from the cortical signal.
source: However, separating physiological from neural sources using an ICA is no guarantee that peripheral physiological activity is fully removed from the cortical signal.
evidence: This is based on the findings showing residual ECG activity after ICA.

claim: Even more sophisticated ICA-based methods that apply wavelet transforms on the ICA components may still not provide a good separation of peripheral physiological and neural activity.
source: Even more sophisticated ICA-based methods that, for example apply wavelet transforms on the ICA components may still not provide a good separation of peripheral physiological and neural activity (Castellanos and Makarov, 2006; Bailey, 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Castellanos and Makarov, 2006 and Bailey, 2024.

claim: The present study indicates that the aperiodic signal recorded using surface sensors/electrodes originates from multiple physiological sources.
source: The present study, focusing on age-related changes in aperiodic neural and cardiac activity, indicates that the aperiodic signal recorded using surface sensors/electrodes originates from multiple physiological sources.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on all the analyses conducted.

claim: Cardiac and neural age-related changes in aperiodic activity vary depending on the frequency range and recording site.
source: Cardiac and neural age-related changes in aperiodic activity vary depending on the frequency range and recording site.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion based on the frequency- and location-dependent analyses.

claim: Conflating cardiac and neural contributions to aperiodic activity obstructs our understanding of both neural and cardiac aperiodic processes and should be avoided.
source: Conflating cardiac and neural contributions to aperiodic activity obstructs our understanding of both neural and cardiac aperiodic processes and should be avoided.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.
